strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem—proving whether sensitive/copyrighted documents were used in LLM fine-tuning—under a realistic black-box threat model where prior signals (MIAs, verbatim regurgitation) are known to be unreliable.

The cue-reply design using invisible Unicode syllables is a clean, genuinely text-preserving marking scheme: it leaves visible content byte-for-byte intact, avoids the invasive 'trap' insertion of prior work, and the syllable/tokenization-level design choices (m=4, single-token characters) are well-motivated empirically.

The ranking test against reserved counterfactual watermarks yields a provable FPR bound (FPR ≤ k/K), and the paper correctly identifies and adopts the conditions from Zhang et al. needed to make such a bound valid; the cryptographic commitment to watermark choice at assignment time is a thoughtful safeguard against cherry-picking.

The experimental evaluation is systematic along the relevant axes: collection size, training set size (down to 0.33% marked data), and number of concurrent unique watermarks, across two models and two text domains; the 18,000+ challenge ranking evaluation with zero spurious detections is a meaningful empirical validation.

The limitations discussion is honest and specific (brittleness to sanitization/OCR/paraphrasing, reliance on a TTP, scope restricted to adapter-based fine-tuning, legal/ethical caveats about altering byte representation), and code and evaluation scripts are promised for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Scope of empirical validation is narrow: only LoRA fine-tuning of two 7B open-weight models on two modest datasets. The authors themselves note that pretraining, RLHF, and full fine-tuning may dilute the signal, so the central claim of reliable provenance auditing is only established for a restricted regime that is favorable to memorization.

Practical robustness is a significant open weakness: the watermark is trivially destroyed by any sanitization that strips zero-width characters—an adversary scraping text at scale could plausibly apply such filtering. The paper acknowledges this but offers no adversarial experiments, and the mitigation sketch (fuzzy matching, error-correcting codes) is deferred entirely to future work.

The novelty is moderate: it is essentially a careful combination of well-known components—Unicode-whitespace steganography (UniSpaCh, Innamark), canary memorization/regurgitation (Carlini et al.), and the counterfactual ranking test (Carlini; Zhang et al.). The cue-reply split and chunked embedding are sensible engineering contributions rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The soundness argument relies on the assumption that invisible marks 'are unlikely to impact the production of subsequent documents by third parties'; this is asserted rather than tested, and the empirical FPR analysis (Section IV.E) is a rough back-of-envelope calculation rather than a rigorous statistical treatment.

Several evaluation aspects are thin: five runs per configuration, small λ values, ranking tests in only four model-dataset settings, and a possible typo in Algorithm 1 (line 7 advances x by λ rather than δ, contradicting the surrounding description). Figure 1 is cluttered and hard to parse. Section VI ordering ('We position our work within prior related works in Section VI. Section V discusses...') is awkward.

Per-document detection is weak for some settings (Mistral on Poems has p=0 even at 30 documents; detection rates as low as 30% for LLaMA with 12 watermarks), meaning completeness is far from uniform, which limits the evidentiary value in the legal/forensic contexts the paper motivates.

strengths: The core idea is practical and well-motivated: invisible Unicode canaries with a cue–reply structure enable black-box, text-preserving provenance auditing, which addresses a genuine gap left by MIAs (weak on individual documents) and invasive 'copyright trap' methods.

The verification procedure is designed with soundness in mind: the ranking test against reserved counterfactual watermarks yields an FPR bound (≤ k/K), and the cryptographic commitment at assignment time is a thoughtful mechanism against post-hoc cherry-picking.

The experimental protocol probes the right questions: sensitivity to marked-collection size, training-set size, number of concurrent watermarks, and an explicit ranking-test evaluation (Table III), with per-chunk hit probabilities p and miss probabilities pFN estimated empirically (Table II).

The limitations section is unusually candid: brittleness to normalization/sanitization and active adversaries, reliance on a trusted third party, and restriction to LoRA fine-tuning are all acknowledged, and legal/ethical implications (informed consent, byte-level alteration, evidentiary value) are discussed.
The paper commits to releasing code, watermark generation/detection utilities, and evaluation scripts, and uses open-weight models, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The proposal is essentially a composition of known ingredients: Unicode-whitespace steganography (UniSpaCh, Hellmeier et al.), canary regurgitation testing (Carlini et al.), and the counterfactual ranking test with FPR ≤ k/K borrowed from Zhang et al. [8]. The cue–reply split and interleaved embedding are incremental design choices rather than a new mechanism with new guarantees.

The central guarantee is conditional and weaker than the framing suggests. The FPR bound relies on conditions from [8] (uniform sampling from a candidate set, and the marked data not influencing other published data) that are argued rather than formally established for this setting, and the bound is not novel. 'Soundness' is thus inherited, not contributed.

Fragile detection mechanism. Detection hinges on the model regurgitating exact invisible-character sequences. The method is admitted to be brittle to sanitization pipelines, zero-width filtering, PDF/OCR extraction, and paraphrasing — arguably the default behavior of any competent data ingestion pipeline — so practical completeness is questionable, and only a footnote-level ChatGPT test addresses real API behavior.

Narrow empirical scope. Results cover only two 7B models and two datasets under LoRA fine-tuning with a fixed set of hyperparameters (m=4, n=8, j=5, cr=1, temperature 0.7). No pretraining, no full fine-tuning, no RLHF, no closed-weight models. Completeness varies drastically across settings (per-chunk p ranges from 0.000 to 0.940), so the claimed robustness is model- and dataset-specific.

Detection density is high relative to real deployment: reliable detection requires 30–60 watermarked documents and roughly 11–14 watermark repetitions per text; Mistral/Poems shows zero detection at 30 documents, and the multi-watermark experiment drops to 72% detection in one setting. The headline '45% detection at <0.33% of training data' reflects a favorable configuration.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track paper: several garbled or erroneous sentences (e.g., 'The need for technological support is more evident than the law's inability to ensure legal certainty', 'there occurence', 'quadruple on LLaMA'), an apparent notation collision in Algorithm 1 (line 7 uses λ for the chunk offset while λ elsewhere denotes the query repetition factor), typographical errors in the appendix ('Samlpe True'), and a section ordering in the outline (related work in VI discussed before limitations in V) that does not match the introduction's stated flow.

The trusted-third-party assumption is a significant operational limitation for the envisioned multi-user attribution scenario; the proposed mitigations (append-only logs, blockchains) are deferred to future work without even a preliminary design.

Statistical claims are overstated in places: '100% TPR@0% FPR over 18,000 challenges' is reported as evidence of soundness, but the bounded-FPR ranking test is run only once per configuration (Table III has four rows), and the spurious-detection argument relies on outputs capped at 200 tokens, which artificially limits the chance of a coincidental reply.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and timely problem (post-hoc auditing of whether sensitive/copyrighted texts were used to fine-tune LLMs) with a design that genuinely satisfies a niche currently unserved in the literature: text-preserving (visible-text-unchanged), black-box, multi-watermark provenance auditing. The positioning against MIA-based approaches and against invasive trap/canary methods is well argued and well referenced.

The cue–reply canary construction is a sensible and clean design: splitting a watermark into a stimulus (cue) and a detectable response (reply), embedded in disjoint chunks, enables targeted black-box probing without altering visible text. The analytical treatment of the admissible watermark space (cross-bifix-free constraints, |W| computation) is careful.

The decision procedure is properly grounded: rather than thresholding a raw regurgitation score, the ranking test against reserved counterfactual watermarks inherits a provable FPR bound (≤ k/K) from Zhang et al. [8], and the paper is explicit about the two conditions needed for this bound and includes a cryptographic commitment against post-hoc cherry-picking. This is a more rigorous treatment of soundness than most prior DPA work.

The experimental evaluation is systematic and covers the relevant axes: regurgitation vs. collection size, robustness to training-set size scaling (up to 15k documents, with marked data at <0.33%), multi-watermark interference, and an end-to-end ranking test over ~18,800 challenges yielding the reported 100% TPR@0% FPR. Both models and two text domains are considered, LoRA configuration and generation parameters are fully reported, and code release is promised — good reproducibility.

The limitations section is honest and substantive: brittleness to sanitization/normalization and active adversaries, reliance on a TTP, scope restricted to LoRA fine-tuning, and legal/ethical concerns (integrity of raw bytes, consent, evidentiary value) are all openly discussed rather than hidden. Weak results (e.g., Mistral on Poems with p = 0 at 30 documents, detection drops from 95% to 72% under 12 watermarks) are reported rather than suppressed.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The paper is essentially a careful engineering combination of three known ingredients: invisible-Unicode steganography (UniSpaCh, whitespace steganography), canary regurgitation testing (Carlini et al.), and the counterfactual ranking test with FPR ≤ k/K (Zhang et al. [8], who also provide the theoretical machinery). The cue–reply split and embedding scheme are the main new technical elements; a reviewer could reasonably view the contribution as a well-executed system paper rather than a conceptual advance.

Scope is narrow relative to the motivation. The motivating introduction invokes general-purpose LLMs (GPT, copyright litigation, pretraining-scale opacity), but the method is only evaluated on LoRA fine-tuning of two 7B open models on two small English datasets. The paper concedes that pretraining, RLHF, and full fine-tuning may dilute the signal; as a result, the headline claims about auditing real AI providers are significantly ahead of what is demonstrated. Notably, the method presupposes the data owner can watermark documents before release AND still holds them at audit time, and must re-mark and re-query the entire collection with K−1 counterfactual watermarks — a substantial operational and I/O burden that is under-analyzed.

Robustness is a serious practical weakness. The entire signal lives in zero-width characters that mainstream text pipelines (normalizers, web scrapers, PDF extraction, sanitizers) commonly strip, and an adversary can trivially remove them (or a model could learn to ignore them). The claimed 45% detection at 0.33% contamination holds only under the idealized assumption that invisible characters survive ingestion intact; the paper offers only a single informal ChatGPT observation (footnote 7) that commercial APIs even pass these characters through, leaving the black-box applicability to closed models largely asserted rather than demonstrated.

Some theoretical claims deserve more scrutiny. The FPR ≤ k/K argument requires that the injected marked data 'does not impact other data published afterwards' (condition 2 of [8]); the paper's justification — that wholly invisible marks are 'unlikely to impact the production of subsequent documents' — is plausible but informal. Additionally, the FPR bound covers the ranking decision per watermark, but interactions with per-chunk detection, ties between scores (Algorithm 3 uses ≥), and the multi-document 'any element used' hypothesis are treated somewhat loosely.

Completeness results are heterogeneous and modest in places: per-chunk hit probability p ranges from 0 to 0.94 depending on model/domain, and the abstract's 'above 45%' headline reflects a setting where detection degrades substantially. With only 5 runs per configuration and no confidence intervals on headline numbers, the statistical strength of some claims (e.g., 'failure rate below 0.1%') is thin.

The effective watermark space is smaller than advertised: |W| ≈ 1.86M, and only ~2×10^4 usable watermarks at K = 100, which is far from 'millions to billions' for large-scale multi-user issuance and raises collision/availability concerns at realistic scale. Also, the assumption that all four chosen code points tokenize to a single token is tokenizer-specific and may not transfer to other model families.

Presentation has avoidable blemishes that reduce polish: apparent typos in Algorithm 1 (line 7 'x ← x + λ' where δ is clearly intended), several grammatical errors ('there occurence', 'the dataset size quadruple'), inconsistency between the outline (Section V limitations before VI related work) and the actual ordering, and a Figure 1 that is visually cluttered and hard to parse.
